questions.stem: An analyst prices a plan's yearly budget rows, sets 2029's price to -0.2 and 2030's to 0.5, and reports the resulting L(lam) to the board as a ceiling on any plan's NPV. What is wrong?

options.text: The 2029 and 2030 prices differ by 0.7, so the value may fall below the best plan
options.says: Prices may differ by year; the lesson's best bound came from prices that differ by year, and every price at zero or above gives a ceiling.

options.text: The 2030 price of 0.5 is set too high, so the value may fall below the best plan
options.says: A high price weakens the ceiling but keeps it a ceiling: the lesson's price of 1.0 everywhere still gave a value above the optimum.

options.text: The 2029 price of -0.2 rewards overspending, so the value may fall below the best plan
options.says: Right: the ceiling argument needs the priced term to be at least zero for the optimal plan, which needs every price at zero or above.

options.text: The two prices add up to 0.3, not to 1, so the value may fall below the best plan
options.says: No rule asks prices to sum to one; the lesson's price vectors sum to 1.5, 3 and more and all give ceilings.

origin.section: Any Nonnegative Prices on the Budget Rows Give an Upper Bound

questions.stem: After 40 subgradient iterations on a portfolio, the best Lagrangian bound is 51,200 and the best repaired plan is worth 47,900. The planners' own plan, which meets every rule, is worth 49,000. What does this support?

options.text: The optimum is 47,900, so their plan is 1,100 above the optimum
options.says: A repaired plan is one feasible plan, a lower bound; a feasible plan cannot be above the optimum.

options.text: Their plan is within 2,200 of the optimum, which is at most 51,200
options.says: Right: the bound caps every plan, and their plan is feasible, so the optimum lies between 49,000 and 51,200.

options.text: The optimum is 51,200, so their plan is 2,200 below the optimum
options.says: The bound sits above the optimum: the lesson's bound stayed 2,382.5 above it. It is not the optimum's value.

options.text: Their plan beats 47,900, so it breaks a budget row the repair kept
options.says: Repaired plans are heuristic: the lesson's best repaired plan stayed 891 below the optimum, so a feasible plan can beat them.

origin.section: A Relaxed Plan Repaired Into a Feasible One Gives the Lower Bound

questions.stem: A team relaxes the budget rows of a selection model whose other rows say only 'at most one start per project'. After 500 subgradient iterations the bound stops falling at the LP relaxation's value, well above the best plan. What explains the stall?

options.text: Polyak's steps shrank too fast, so the bound stays at the LP relaxation's value
options.says: The page calls the stall a theorem, not an accident of the step rule: no step rule goes below the Lagrangian dual's value.

options.text: The repaired plans are too weak, so the bound stays at the LP relaxation's value
options.says: The best Lagrangian bound is set by the relaxation; better plans move the lower bound, not the limit of the upper one.

options.text: Some prices went below zero, so the bound stays at the LP relaxation's value
options.says: Each step projects the prices onto zero and above, so no price goes below zero.

options.text: The rows left have an integral LP, so the bound stays at the LP relaxation's value
options.says: Right: with the integrality property the best Lagrangian bound equals the LP bound.

origin.section: When the Pieces' Own LP Has Whole-Number Answers, the Best Bound Is the LP Bound
